cutRule: one part per book (篇); within a book, one unit per stretch of text between Zhu Xi's commentary interruptions; each numbered passage starts a card (ln = passage number, p: true)
sourceStatement: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book {BOOK}, 〈{TITLE}〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.

parts.title: 學而
parts.about: Book 1 of the Analects, 學而 Xué ér, named, as every book is, from its first words ("To learn, and…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this first book records mostly sayings about attending to the root of things — learning, family duty, good faith — as the gateway to the rest. Each numbered passage (1.1–1.16, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 為政
parts.about: Book 2 of the Analects, 為政 Wéi zhèng, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Conducting government…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book begins and ends with government — ruling by virtue and the rites rather than by decree and punishment (2.1, 2.3, 2.19–2.21) — and between them come Confucius' account of his own life decade by decade (2.4), four different answers to the question 'what is filial devotion?' (2.5–2.8), and sayings on learning, knowing, and the gentleman. Each numbered passage (2.1–2.24, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 八佾
parts.about: Book 3 of the Analects, 八佾 Bā yì, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Eight rows (of dancers)…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Almost the whole book is about the rites and music: it opens with Confucius' anger at the great families of Lu who used the king's dances and hymns in their own halls (3.1–3.2), and goes on to what the rites are rooted in (3.3–3.4), sacrifice and the spirits (3.10–3.13), the Zhou dynasty's rites as the model (3.14), archery as a contest of gentlemen (3.7, 3.16), the minister Guan Zhong, great but no master of the rites (3.22), and music — how a performance unfolds (3.23) and the difference between music that is beautiful and music that is also good (3.25). Each numbered passage (3.1–3.26, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 3.9 the edition we follow misprints 把 for 杞, the state of Qi; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 里仁
parts.about: Book 4 of the Analects, 里仁 Lǐ rén, named, as every book is, from its first words ("In a village, humaneness…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Almost every passage in this book is a single short saying of the Master. The first seven all turn on humaneness (仁 rén), the virtue the whole Analects circles: who has it, how rarely it is loved, and how it shows even in a man's faults (4.1–4.7). Then come sayings on the Way and what is right against profit (4.8–4.17), among them the famous exchange in which Confucius tells Master Zeng that one thing runs through his whole Way, and Master Zeng explains it to the others as wholeheartedness and fellow-feeling (4.15); then a group on serving one's parents (4.18–4.21), and short sayings on being slow to speak (4.22–4.24). Each numbered passage (4.1–4.26, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 4.14 the edition we follow misprints 已 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 公冶長
parts.about: Book 5 of the Analects, 公冶長 Gōngyě Cháng, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of a disciple. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this whole book weighs people, ancient and recent, and their worth. It opens with the Master choosing husbands for his daughter and his niece (5.1), and goes on to his verdicts on his own disciples: Zigong a precious vessel (5.3), Zilu's daring outrunning his judgement (5.6), three disciples each fit for office yet not called humane (5.7), Yan Hui able to work out ten things from one (5.8), Zai Yu caught asleep in the daytime (5.9). Then it turns to men of the age before him — statesmen of Lu, Qi, Chu, Wei and Zheng (5.14–5.20) and the ancient worthies Boyi and Shuqi (5.22) — asking of each whether he was humane, a word the Master almost never grants. It closes with the Master and two disciples each stating what they hope for (5.25) and a last saying on the love of learning (5.27). Each numbered passage (5.1–5.27, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In two places the edition we follow misprints a character (宰子 for the disciple 宰予 in 5.9, 已 for 己 'oneself' in 5.15); the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 雍也
parts.about: Book 6 of the Analects, 雍也 Yōng yě, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Yong…", the personal name of the disciple Ran Yong). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi notes that the first half of this book goes on as Book 5 did, weighing people: Ran Yong fit to face south as a ruler (6.1), Yan Hui the one disciple who truly loved learning, dead young (6.2), and never straying from humaneness for three months together (6.5), content in a poor lane with a basket of rice and a gourd of water (6.9); the Master grieving at the bedside of the sick Bo Niu (6.8), and telling Ran Qiu that he has drawn his own line before his strength ran out (6.10). The second half gathers some of the most quoted sayings in the book: plain stuff and pattern in balance (6.16), knowing a thing, loving it and delighting in it (6.18), the wise delighting in water and the humane in mountains (6.21), the gu vessel that is no longer a gu (6.23), the Master's visit to Nanzi, the notorious wife of the ruler of Wei, and his oath to the offended Zilu (6.26), the virtue of the constant mean (6.27), and to close, what humaneness is: wishing to stand oneself, setting others up (6.28). Each numbered passage (6.1–6.28, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 6.28 the edition we follow misprints 已 and 巳 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 述而
parts.about: Book 7 of the Analects, 述而 Shù ér, named, as every book is, from its first words ("transmitting, and…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this book mostly records the Master's words about himself, always modest ones, and his teaching, together with what he was like and what he did. It opens with him calling himself a transmitter, not a maker (7.1), and dreaming no longer of the Duke of Zhou (7.5); it shows him at ease at home (7.4), refusing to eat his fill beside the bereaved (7.9), so carried away by the Shao music in Qi that for three months he did not notice the taste of meat (7.13), content with coarse rice, water and a bent arm for a pillow (7.15), and sure that Heaven's gift in him was beyond the reach of a man who wanted him dead (7.22). Some of the most quoted lines of the whole Analects are here: the Master not speaking of prodigies, feats of strength, disorder or spirits (7.20), finding a teacher in any two companions on the road (7.21), humaneness arriving the moment one wants it (7.29), and the gentleman calm and broad where the small man is forever anxious (7.36). The book closes on a picture of him: warm yet stern, commanding without harshness, respectful and at ease (7.37). Each numbered passage (7.1–7.37, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 7.28 the edition we follow misprints 已 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 泰伯
parts.about: Book 8 of the Analects, 泰伯 Tàibó, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Taibo"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book opens and closes with the sage rulers of old: Taibo, who three times gave up the succession to Zhou so quietly that no one could praise him for it (8.1), Yao, Shun and Yu, who held the world without making it their own (8.18–8.19), the few great ministers of Shun and King Wu (8.20), and Yu, who ate and dressed poorly and spent his strength on the field channels (8.21). Between them come Master Zeng's last words — showing his disciples hands and feet kept unharmed (8.3), and the dying man's words that are good (8.4) — and his picture of the officer, broad and resolute, whose charge is heavy and whose road is far, laid down only at death (8.7); the Master's three stages of learning — roused by the Odes, standing firm by the rites, made complete by music (8.8); his saying that the people can be brought to go by it but not to know it (8.9); and his advice to keep out of a state in peril and hide when the Way does not prevail (8.13). Each numbered passage (8.1–8.21, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 8.4 the edition we follow misprints 地 for 也; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 子罕
parts.about: Book 9 of the Analects, 子罕 Zǐ hǎn, named, as every book is, from its first words ("The Master seldom…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Much of this book is about the Master himself as others saw him and as he saw himself: the four things he was wholly free of (9.4); his calm when surrounded and threatened at Kuang, sure that Heaven had not meant the heritage of King Wen to perish with him (9.5); his answer to those who wondered at his many skills — he had been poor and humble when young (9.6); his rebuke of Zilu for dressing up disciples as the household officers of a great man he no longer was (9.11); and his musings on selling a fine jade (9.12) and on going to live among the eastern tribes (9.13). Yan Yuan sighs that the Master's Way rises higher the more he looks up at it (9.10). There are many short sayings much quoted since: the river flowing on day and night (9.16), never having met anyone who loved virtue as he loved beauty (9.17), the young who are to be feared, since no one can know they will not match the present (9.22), the common man whose will cannot be taken from him (9.25), the pine and cypress that are last to wither when the year turns cold (9.27), and the wise, the humane and the brave (9.28). Each numbered passage (9.1–9.30, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 9.5 and 9.11 the edition we follow misprints 子 for 予 'I, me'; the reading text is corrected and the notes say so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 鄉黨
parts.about: Book 10 of the Analects, 鄉黨 Xiāng dǎng, named, as every book is, from its first words ("In his home village…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book is unlike the others: it is hardly sayings at all, but a picture of the Master in his daily life, set down by people who watched him closely — how he spoke at home and at court, how he carried himself before his lord and as an envoy abroad, what he wore in each season, how he fasted, what he would and would not eat, how he sat, slept and rode in a chariot. Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: what the sage called the Way is never apart from everyday use, and so his disciples noted his every movement; and Yin Tun: reading it now, the sage seems to stand before your eyes — though he did not hold himself in by rule, his virtue was simply so full that every gesture met the rites of itself. Much of the detail is old court ritual, explained briefly in the notes from the commentaries. Two lines are among the best known in the book: when the stables burned, he asked whether anyone was hurt, and did not ask about the horses (10.12); and the closing lines on the hen pheasant on the hill bridge (10.18), which Zhu Xi thought must have lost some words. Zhu Xi prints the whole book as one chapter cut into sections; each section (10.1–10.18, as the edition marks them) begins a new card, and longer sections are cut where his commentary interrupts the text. Many modern editions divide the book more finely, into 27. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.
parts.note: Zhu Xi prints 鄉黨 as one chapter (舊說凡一章) and says he divides it into 17 sections (今分為十七節), but the Siku copy marks 18 ○ breaks; passages = the 18 printed sections (10.1–10.18). See QUESTIONS.md.
